prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part, B040, credited to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the scientific chain, which none of us disputes: proglucagon processing, the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, its glucose-dependent insulinotropic and appetite actions in humans, receptor biology, and independent confirmation in large randomized outcome trials for glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. The question the chair raises, whether the object of the prize is the physiology or the drug, is the decisive judgement, and I answer it as before: the discovery of what the hormone is and does is what the prize should honour, and the pharmaceutical step rests on it. I also see no scientific reason to add a second part. A second achievement would force a split of the three-person limit and thin the B040 credit, and none of the candidates offered as partners (B034, B039, B008, B025) is stronger on maturity and exact credit than the GLP-1 case.
statement.case_against: The weakness remains attribution. Mojsov's priority on the active peptide is credited but contested, Habener-group work lies outside the credited names, and Knudsen, whose long-acting analogues are what patients receive, is excluded by the three-person cap. I cannot adjudicate the primary-literature priority from the supplied evidence, so my confidence is higher in the topic than in the exact trio. If a majority concluded that the analogue design was the decisive step, Knudsen would have to take a place and I would then ask which physiology name has the weakest claim, which I would not want to answer without the primary record. The citation should say plainly that the absence of Knudsen and Habener is a framing choice about what the discovery was, not a judgement of their importance. Long-term durability and safety of weight-loss effects are still being characterised, although this does not touch the discovery itself.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks that the citation make the exclusion of Knudsen an explicit framing choice, resists a four-name prize, and does not want the Rosenberg question on CAR-T decided by name count alone.
responses.response: I agree on the citation wording and have tightened mine so that it names the physiology and the active peptide as the object of the prize. On Rosenberg I concede part of the point: adoptive cell transfer and the first gene-engineered T-cell trials are a real antecedent, and counting names is not an argument. My reason for a narrow CAR-T citation is the scope of the claim. If B034 is ever considered, the citation should be about the engineered-receptor concept and its clinical realisation, and that is where Eshhar's absence is a larger problem than Rosenberg's inclusion or exclusion. I also accept her point that CAR-T has moved into autoimmune disease, and it makes me rank B034 above optogenetics as a fallback.

responses.point: Perlmann rates B039 as the strongest basic-science alternative with a clean Mori and Walter credit, and the chair asks whether a citation limited to the IRE1/HAC1/XBP1 arm is defensible.
responses.response: I take the credit argument seriously, and a citation worded narrowly, for the discovery of the signalling pathway from the endoplasmic reticulum to the nucleus through IRE1, unconventional splicing and the transcriptional response, is defensible even though the PERK arm (Ron, Harding, Kaufman) is not represented. That narrowness is a cost the committee would have to state openly. Where I still differ is on weighting. Clean credit and mechanistic completeness make B039 a good prize in the abstract, but it does not outweigh a discovery whose consequence for patients is already measured in randomized trials. I have moved B039 into my alternatives in place of optogenetics because, if B040 stalled on attribution, it is the fallback whose credit I could defend most readily. I still see it as a candidate that will not weaken by waiting.

responses.point: The chair asks whether a single-achievement B040 is preferred to a two-part prize, and which of B034, B039, B008 or B025 would be the better partner and how the three names would be divided.
responses.response: I prefer the single part. With a cap of three people over the whole configuration, a second part leaves at most one or two names for B040 and I cannot see a division that does not damage the GLP-1 credit by dropping Mojsov, Holst or Drucker. If the committee nevertheless wants two parts, the best partner would be B034 as June with Sadelain, which would leave only one name for B040 and make a poor trade. I also note your correction of the imatinib rank. My own round-1 text called B043 seventh, so I rely on the opening record rather than memory. My reservation about B043 does not depend on the rank: the BCR-ABL lesion lies outside the credited trio, so the prize would honour validation of a principle.

responses.point: El-Manira, using circuit-dissection tools himself, keeps optogenetics (B008) as an alternative because six credited names face a three-person limit, and says a second part is more plausible than in his opening ballot.
responses.response: I agree that optogenetics is the hardest attribution problem on the shortlist. Any trio leaves out Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenbock, and I still separate the molecular discovery of channelrhodopsin function (Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg) from the neuronal demonstration (Boyden, Deisseroth, Miesenbock), which a trio cannot represent. That is why I drop B008 from my alternatives for this round. I do not dismiss it as a method, and the Nobel tradition has honoured methods, but its medical translation is early and the credit cannot be drawn cleanly today. I do not share the view that a second part is more attractive now. It adds no clarity to the B040 credit.

responses.point: Sandberg would reconsider the B040 trio only if the committee judged drug design decisive, and argues that the Nobel tradition has repeatedly honoured enabling methods.
responses.response: I agree with the conditional. The structure of the decision is simple: if the prize is about the discovery of the hormone's actions, the trio stands; if it is about the medicines, Knudsen replaces someone and the case changes. I find the first reading more defensible. On methods I agree that tradition is not an argument against B008, and I weigh it on maturity and attribution, where it is difficult for the reasons given above. We have eight co-authored works together, none involving a credited name on the shortlist, so my agreement with you here is on the science and does not rest on that.

uncertainties: How to weigh Mojsov's contested priority against Habener-group work, which is not among the credited names, without access to the primary record.
Whether Knudsen should replace one of the three physiology names if a majority treats analogue design as the decisive step, and which name would give way.
Whether the narrow IRE1/HAC1/XBP1 citation for B039 or the engineered-receptor citation for B034 could be made accurate given the PERK and ATF6 contributors and Eshhar's absence.
Long-term durability and safety of weight-loss effects and cost-effectiveness of GLP-1 therapy are still being characterised.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented tie to any credited name on the shortlist. My research on single-cell genomics, spatial transcriptomics and brain atlases is unrelated to B040, B034 and B039. I have eight recorded co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg, none involving a credited shortlist name. I infer no personal ties from shared institutions.
